item.title: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026
item.dc:creator: Guido van Rossum
item.description:
I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15.

It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that.

Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing.

Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink>) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”.

At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work.

In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort: a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android.

Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs,

–Guido

item.title: Is CPython sovereignty at risk?
item.dc:creator: Facundo Batista
item.description:
Bear with me, a bit of history…

  1. A company built a piece of software in the shadows and announces it publicly. This software provides a drop-in replacement for other common and standard community-maintained tools that have been around for years.

  2. The company’s piece of software is N times faster than the community one and behaves slightly differently in edge cases most people never noticed.

  3. Due to its speed, it’s adopted by most of community worldwide sparking debate about being a company-developed software that the PSF and community don’t control. However, “it’s open-source and we can fork it if we don’t like that company anymore”.

  4. Release after release, the company builds trust on hundred of contributors of the community, making the adoption to continue growing.

  5. A few years after building that trust on the community members, the same company released a piece of software 100% AI-developed, using the latest frontier models, burning an undisclosed quantity of tokens, and makes a big public announcement. This software is a faster CPython bytecode compiler and it’s also open-source. The code is so complex that no human can understand it.

Will the community adopt this faster CPython bytecode compiler? Who owns this piece of software? Who understands this software? Who are the ones with access to those latest frontier models with millions of tokens to burn and fix a bug on that software?

The idea behind “we can fork it if the company becomes evil” doesn’t work anymore. The community may not have access to those frontier models that can understand the code generated by the company, or it may be prohibitively expensive to use them for further maintenance of the project.

An AI company that creates the frontier models with unlimited access to tokens to burn and decides who can access to which models puts the CPython sovereignty at risk.

Context: Charlie Marsh on X: "I had Codex build a CPython bytecode compiler in Rust (`serc`). It emits byte-for-byte identical output on the top 10,000 PyPI packages, 2-4x faster than the CPython implementation. This was entirely an experiment, though we may ship it (opt-in) in uv." / X

.
Facundo Batista
Manuel Kaufmann (@humitos)
